info.description:
# Merged Masterclass Backend - All APIs

GENERATED from the live URLconf by `Miscellaneous/Scripts/generate_postman_collection.py` on 2026-09-30.
Do not hand-edit: re-run the script after any routing change.

**151 mounted API routes** -> **158 requests** across **19 folders**. The Django admin UI is excluded; it is not an API surface.

Request bodies: 50 of 62 write endpoints carry a template generated from the view's own validator. The rest either take no body by design (stated on the request) or use a pattern the generator does not yet read.

## Breaking changes, shipped 2026-09-24

Re-import rather than merging. A client built before this date still calls paths that MOVED, and the old ones 404 with no redirect shim.

- **Maintenance split three ways (2026-09-24).** `account/app-maintainance/` -> `app-api/v1/account/maintainance-status/`, `account/web/app-status/` -> `web-api/v1/account/maintainance-status/`, and the staff POST toggle moved to `account/universal/maintainance-status/`. Both probes are now anonymous and answer the same two keys, `is_maintenance` and `force_logout_all_user`.
- **The web probe lost three keys.** `is_web_maintenance` is now `is_maintenance`; `is_pathway` and `is_onboarding_completed` are gone from it entirely - `GET account/user-details/` already answers both.
- **`account/user_details/` (underscore) was DELETED**, along with its PATCH. `account/user-details/` (hyphen) is the only one left and is GET-only; write profile fields through `PATCH account/profile/`.
- **Six lead-capture routes** now file a Salesforce enquiry: `talk-to-us/`, `enquiry/`, and the four programme funnels under `caira/`, `cpa/` and `cma/`. The four funnels take NO body - any key is a 400.

## Setup

1. Import all four files and select the LOCAL, UAT or PROD environment.
2. Set `login_identifier` to the e-mail or phone you are testing with.
3. Send **POST auth-otp-send-v1**, put the code you receive in `otp_code`, then send **POST auth-otp-verify-v1**.

That is the whole setup. `token` and `refresh_token` are written by the scripts - do not paste a token in by hand, and do not expect one to survive a logout.

Webhook requests are the exception: they are `noauth` and carry their own secret header, so set `lms_notification_webhook_key` and `miles_one_webhook_secret` for **19. Inbound Webhooks (no JWT)**.

## What runs automatically

Everything below is Postman-side scripting. There is no companion runner and nothing writes to disk; the environment is the only state.

- **The access token renews itself.** The collection pre-request script reads `exp` out of the JWT and refreshes when fewer than `token_refresh_skew_seconds` (120) remain. Refresh tokens ROTATE, so the new pair is stored immediately - which is also why nothing here ever refreshes twice at once. Set `auto_refresh` to `off` to stop it.
- **Path parameters fill themselves.** After any 2xx JSON response the collection test script walks the body and writes any key matching a path variable into the environment, so a list request sets up the detail request that follows it. `id` is deliberately NOT harvested - it is the path parameter of one route (the certificate webhook) and the commonest key in every list body, so set it by hand. It fills a variable ONLY WHEN THAT VARIABLE IS EMPTY, so a value you pinned yourself is never overwritten - clear it if you want it re-harvested. Set `auto_capture` to `off` to stop it. Only the FIRST element of a list is read, and only keys named exactly like the path variable.
- **Every response is checked for the baseline**: no 5xx, and a JSON content type parses. Response time is logged, never asserted - it is a property of the machine the run is on.
- **A 401 or 403 explains itself** in the console instead of leaving a bare status code: whether a token is set at all, and whether a webhook secret rather than a token is what the route wanted.
- **The three session routes carry their own scripts** - verify stores the minted pair, refresh stores the rotated pair, logout clears both, and only on a 2xx.

Query parameters are present but DISABLED, so a request sends nothing it was not asked to send.

## What each request tells you

Open any request's Documentation pane. It carries the view and permission behind the route, the body it accepts, the query parameters it declares, every error `code` it can return and what each one means, and the shape of the response - taken from the contracts the frontend web team works to. There is no separate documentation folder to go and read: the detail is on the request you are about to send.

## Saved examples

Every request carries saved examples - 822 of them, 5.2 per request - one per outcome that request can produce. Pick them from the dropdown beside Send to see the success body, each validation failure, the authentication refusal and the 500 envelope without having to provoke them.

**They are READ OFF THE HANDLER, not written by hand.** Each one comes from a `Response(...)` in the view's own source - including the ones built in a shared helper or in the function the handler delegates to - so when a handler changes shape the examples change with it on the next run. A saved example is the part of a collection that normally rots first, and a tester comparing a live 400 against a stale example cannot tell which of the two is wrong.

**A value in angle brackets was not invented.** `"user_id": "<str(user_id)>"` means the key is there and the script could not resolve its value from the source - it shows you where the value comes from instead of fabricating one that would look like a format guarantee. The response SHAPE in those cases is in the contract text further down the same pane.

**Status codes with no example are not outcomes that cannot happen.** A route whose response is proxied from an upstream service carries that service's status, which is not readable from this side - the five sign-in routes are the case in point, and their success bodies are documented in the contract text instead.

## Folders

- **01. Authentication and Session** - 5 routes, 5 requests (5 UNIVERSAL).
- **02. Account, Profile and Reference Content** - 19 routes, 22 requests (3 APP, 15 UNIVERSAL, 1 WEB).
- **03. Masterclass - Learning Flow (app)** - 29 routes, 29 requests (28 APP, 1 WEBHOOK).
- **04. Masterclass - Learning Flow (web)** - 23 routes, 23 requests (23 WEB).
- **05. AI Labs** - 5 routes, 5 requests (5 UNIVERSAL).
- **06. Events and Bookings** - 18 routes, 18 requests (8 APP, 6 UNIVERSAL, 4 WEB).
- **07. CAIRA - Badges, Certificates, CPE** - 1 routes, 1 requests (1 UNIVERSAL).
- **08. Notifications and Bell** - 5 routes, 5 requests (5 UNIVERSAL).
- **09. Catalogue** - 11 routes, 11 requests (11 UNIVERSAL).
- **10. Commerce** - 7 routes, 11 requests (7 UNIVERSAL).
- **11. Engagement - Likes, Saves, Watches** - 2 routes, 2 requests (2 UNIVERSAL).
- **14. Varun Masterclass** - 6 routes, 6 requests (6 APP).
- **15. Learn Page (app)** - 1 routes, 1 requests (1 APP).
- **16. Home Page (app)** - 2 routes, 2 requests (2 APP).
- **17. Badges - CPE Tracker (app and web)** - 6 routes, 6 requests (3 APP, 2 UNIVERSAL, 1 WEB).
- **18. Webinar Feedback (app and web)** - 4 routes, 4 requests (2 APP, 2 WEB).
- **19. Inbound Webhooks (no JWT)** - 3 routes, 3 requests (3 WEBHOOK).
- **20. Referral** - 3 routes, 3 requests (2 UNIVERSAL, 1 WEBHOOK).
- **21. Favourites (app)** - 1 routes, 1 requests (1 APP).

## Conventions that apply to every request

> From `ACCOUNTS_API_CONTRACT_V1.md` - the contract the frontend web team works to.



## 1. Conventions

### 1.1 Every path moved under `account/`, and there is no redirect

Ported paths were namespaced under `account/` on 2026-08-12. Django does not treat `faqs` and
`account/faqs` as the same route, so an un-updated build gets a **404, not a redirect**. No shim exists.

Two legacy oddities are reproduced on purpose and are not typos to fix on your side:

- `maintainance` is **misspelt** in all three maintenance paths, matching `settings.APP_UNDER_MAINTENANCE`'s
  readers. It stays: a path that spells it correctly next to settings that do not is worse than one
  consistent mistake.
- Every path now carries a trailing slash, including `country` and `faqs`, which did not have one in legacy.

### 1.2 Authentication

`Authorization: Bearer <jwt>` where the table says JWT. A **bad or expired token answers `403`, not `401`** -
DRF downgrades an authentication failure when the authenticator does not implement `authenticate_header()`, and
ours does not. Do not key token-refresh on 401 alone.

The endpoints marked "enforced in handler" are a different shape: they carry no permission class, so an
anonymous request reaches the handler and gets a **401** from an explicit check inside it. So on those four you
can see 401 for anonymous and 403 for a broken token, from the same route.

### 1.3 Undeclared keys are rejected

Request bodies and query strings are validated strictly. A key the endpoint does not declare is a 400 naming
it. Sending a known key as `null` is also rejected where the field does not allow null - strict validation
forbids the key's *presence*, so "send it as null to be safe" does not work.

### 1.4 Error envelopes

The auth proxy routes (section 2) return **the SSO's own body, whole and untouched**, whatever it contains.
Everything this backend generates itself uses one of:

```json
{ "message": "Sign-in is temporarily unavailable. Please try again." }
{ "code": "account_blocked", "message": "This account has been blocked..." }
{ "message": "Invalid request.", "details": { "country": ["..."] } }
```

DRF validation failures on the serializer-backed routes come back as DRF's native shape - a map of field name
to a list of messages - not the `{status, code, errors[]}` envelope the Events routes use. **The two apps do
not share an error shape.** Handle both.

---

## 2. The login flow

Five routes, in order. All five are proxies onto the Miles SSO auth API: they OBTAIN a token, they do not
verify one. Verification is local, against the issuer's JWKS, on every subsequent request.

```
auth-identify  ->  auth-otp-send  ->  auth-otp-verify  ->  (session)
                                                             |
                                            auth-token-refresh (rotate)
                                                             |
                                                       auth-logout
```

## 6. Maintenance probes

RESTRUCTURED 2026-09-24, and this is a **breaking change on three counts**: both probe paths moved,
the web payload lost three keys and renamed a fourth, and the POST toggle moved to a third route.
There is no shim; an un-updated build 404s on the first call it makes.

| was | is |
| --- | --- |
| `GET account/app-maintainance/` | `GET app-api/v1/account/maintainance-status/` |
| `GET account/web/app-status/` | `GET web-api/v1/account/maintainance-status/` |
| `POST account/app-maintainance/` | `POST account/universal/maintainance-status/` |

### 8.2 The two apps do not share an error shape

Events returns `{status, code, errors[]}` and asks you to switch on `code`. Accounts returns DRF's native
validation shape, a bare `{message}`, or the SSO's body untouched. There is no single error parser that covers
both. See 1.4.

### 8.3 The auth routes return the SSO's body, not ours

Everything on the five auth routes except the two local flags and the refusals listed in 2.3 is passed through
from the Miles SSO verbatim, including fields not documented here. Treat unknown keys as additive, and do not
assume our version pins their schema.

## 1. Conventions

### 1.1 Three path prefixes, and the split is deliberate

- `api/v1/events/...` - SHARED. The registration handshake. One write path, one contract, one set of side
  effects (Zoom -> Booking -> Salesforce). A web caller and an app caller register identically.
- `web-api/v1/events/...` - WEB-ONLY READS. The landing feed and the detail page behind it.
- `app-api/v1/events/...` - APP-ONLY READS. The bookings feed.

What a page renders is genuinely surface-shaped: bucket counts, ordering and payload width differ between a
browser and a phone, so a read belongs to the surface that renders it. No route has a twin on the other read
prefix yet.

The rule this encodes: writes stay shared, reads split by surface.

`app-api/` was added on 2026-09-17 and `all-bookings/` moved onto it. An earlier version of this document
described that route as web-only; that was wrong, and the prefix is the part of this scheme that names the
surface, so it was corrected rather than left. It was MOVED, not aliased - this document went out the same
day, so there is no shipped client on the old path.

Note that `Masterclass` splits web from app a DIFFERENT way, by domain segment (`api/v1/masterclass/` vs
`api/v1/masterclass-web/`). Which scheme a surface uses is a fact to look up, not to derive.

### 1.2 Authentication

`Authorization: Bearer <jwt>` on every route above, except `webinar-main-page?login_type=pre_login`, which is
served anonymously.

**`webinar-details-page` TAKES NO `login_type` AND IS NOT GATED.** It derives the surface from the request:
send a token and you get the post-login page with its `registration` block, send none and you get the
pre-login page without it. A signed-out visitor can open a webinar page.

**CHANGED 2026-09-18.** It shipped on 2026-09-17 as `IsAuthenticated`, answering `403` to anonymous callers.
If you built against that, the 403 is gone and `data.login_type` now tells you which surface you received.

A BAD OR EXPIRED TOKEN ANSWERS `403`, NOT `401`. This is true of every authenticated route in this backend,
not just these four: DRF downgrades an authentication failure to 403 when the authenticator does not implement
`authenticate_header()`, and ours does not. Do not key token-refresh logic on 401 alone. The one `401` this app
returns is a different case entirely - see section 6.2.

### 1.3 Undeclared parameters are rejected, not ignored

Every request body and query string is validated strictly. A key the endpoint does not declare is a 400 naming
that key; it is not silently dropped. A typo'd filter therefore fails loudly instead of returning an
unfiltered 200.

### 1.4 Error envelopes

Validation failure (400):

```json
{
  "status": "error",
  "code": "invalid_request",
  "errors": [{ "field": "login_type", "message": "Field required" }]
}
```

`field` is dot-joined, so a bad key inside a list element reads as `chapters.0.chapter_id`. An undeclared key
comes back with that key as `field`.

Domain refusal (400 / 404 / 409):

```json
{ "status": "error", "code": "webinar_not_found", "detail": "Webinar does not exist." }
```

SWITCH ON `code`, NEVER ON THE HTTP STATUS AND NEVER ON `detail`. The `code` values are the stable contract;
wording and status can move.

One inconsistency to handle before you write the error handler: the `authentication_required` refusal from
`webinar-main-page` carries `message` where every other refusal carries `detail`. Read `detail ?? message`.

### 1.5 Status codes are real

The legacy V4 register endpoint answered `500` for every input and state problem, because FE reserved 400/404
for token-refresh and logout flows. These routes return the real `400` / `404` / `409` / `401`. If an
interceptor still treats any 4xx as a session problem, that has to change before you point at these routes.
A client that switches on `code` rather than on status needs no change.

---

**Surface:** UNIVERSAL  
**View:** `AuthIdentifyViewV1`  
**Module:** `Accounts.views`  
**Route name:** `auth-identify-v1`  
**Methods on this view:** POST  
**Authentication:** none  
**Permission:** AllowAny

POST - how does this person authenticate?

Body template generated from `AuthIdentifyRequestSerializerV1`. Values are placeholders, not fixtures.

Some values are ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES rather than placeholders - set `login_identifier` once and the three sign-in requests all read it. `refresh_token` is written by a script; do not type it.

---

> From `ACCOUNTS_API_CONTRACT_V1.md` - the contract the frontend web team works to.



### 2.1 `POST auth-identify/` - how does this person authenticate?

The first call of any login, always.

```json
{ "identifier": "learner@example.com" }
```

`identifier` is an email, phone number or username - the SSO works out which. `appCode` is **not accepted from
the client**; it is added server-side, because it names which application is asking and a caller must not be
able to claim to be another one.

The response is the SSO's, and carries `methods`, `defaultMethod`, masked destinations and `communicationId`.

**Render `methods` rather than assuming a form.** When enterprise SSO ships, this same endpoint starts
answering `saml` with a redirect. A client that renders the list needs no change; one that hardcoded an OTP box
needs a rewrite.

**Do not build a "no such account" message from this response.** An identifier the SSO has never seen returns
the same `methods`, `defaultMethod` and masks as a known one - the masks are built from what was typed, not
from anything stored. There is no negative signal here to render, by design.

This route discloses account existence through `communicationId` (null for an unknown identifier), which is why
it is **first-party only** and the most tightly throttled of the five at 20/min. Do not expose it to an
untrusted origin.

**Route name:** `auth-logout-v1`  
**Methods on this view:** POST

POST - end the session at the SSO.

**No request body by design.** Bearer header only; the SSO reads the token, not a body.

**This request carries its own test script** on top of the collection-level one - open the Scripts tab to read what it writes into the environment.

---

> From `ACCOUNTS_API_CONTRACT_V1.md` - the contract the frontend web team works to.



### 2.5 `POST auth-logout/` - end the session at the SSO

Empty body. Takes the bearer from the inbound `Authorization` header and forwards it.

Missing or non-Bearer header is a 401 with
`{"message": "Authorization header with a Bearer token is required."}`.

Note this deliberately does **not** resolve the token to a local user first: logout must work for a token this
database has no row for, because a session worth ending still exists.

**Surface:** UNIVERSAL  
**View:** `AuthOtpSendViewV1`  
**Module:** `Accounts.views`  
**Route name:** `auth-otp-send-v1`  
**Methods on this view:** POST  
**Authentication:** none  
**Permission:** AllowAny

**Replaces legacy MilesOne** `POST login-with-phone-otp`

POST - send a one-time code.

Body template generated from `AuthOtpSendRequestSerializerV1`. Values are placeholders, not fixtures.

Some values are ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES rather than placeholders - set `login_identifier` once and the three sign-in requests all read it. `refresh_token` is written by a script; do not type it.

---

> From `ACCOUNTS_API_CONTRACT_V1.md` - the contract the frontend web team works to.



### 2.2 `POST auth-otp-send/` - send a one-time code

```json
{ "identifier": "learner@example.com" }
```

The response carries `channel` and `cooldownSeconds`.

**Write UI copy from the returned `channel`, never from what you sent.** It is `email`, `sms` or `whatsapp`,
and phone routing is a table at the SSO that changes with no deploy on either side. **As of 2026-09-08 every
country resolves to `sms`, India included** - WhatsApp routing is off until delivery is proved end to end.

`cooldownSeconds` is how long the resend button stays disabled. Read it; do not hardcode one.

`channel` is **not accepted as an input** yet. The SSO takes it as an optional override, but this route does not
declare it, so sending it is a 400.

**A `503` means nothing was sent and nothing will be.** The identity store accepted the request and then
refused to deliver. Advance the user to a retry, never to a code-entry screen. It says our mailer is broken -
it never says anything about the account. Every identifier-specific outcome is a 200.

One caveat on phone identifiers: they are proxied faithfully rather than refused, so a **well-formed Indian
phone number can reach a silent failure** - the provider accepts the SMS and the carrier drops it, so a 200 does
not prove a message arrived. The client is currently the only thing preventing that. A *malformed* number is
not your problem: the SSO answers 400 with copy written for a learner, and that message reaches the phone field
unaltered - render it.

**Surface:** UNIVERSAL  
**View:** `AuthOtpVerifyViewV1`  
**Module:** `Accounts.views`  
**Route name:** `auth-otp-verify-v1`  
**Methods on this view:** POST  
**Authentication:** none  
**Permission:** AllowAny

**Replaces legacy MilesOne** `POST verify-otp`

POST - exchange a one-time code for a session.

Body template generated from `AuthOtpVerifyRequestSerializerV1`. Values are placeholders, not fixtures.

Some values are ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES rather than placeholders - set `login_identifier` once and the three sign-in requests all read it. `refresh_token` is written by a script; do not type it.

**This request carries its own test script** on top of the collection-level one - open the Scripts tab to read what it writes into the environment.

---

> From `ACCOUNTS_API_CONTRACT_V1.md` - the contract the frontend web team works to.



### 2.3 `POST auth-otp-verify/` - exchange the code for a session

```json
{ "identifier": "learner@example.com", "code": "123456" }
```

`code` is a **string, and its length is not validated here**. The code length is set server-side at the SSO -
read it rather than hardcoding six boxes.

On success the body carries `accessToken` and `refreshToken`. For a web client the SSO **also** sets the
httpOnly `miles_sso_refresh` cookie, which is forwarded verbatim.

Two **local** flags are merged into the success body, and they are the reason this route is worth reading
carefully. Neither is in the token, and the SSO knows nothing about either:

| Key | Values | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `profile_status` | `new_user`, `onboard_completed`, `profile_completed` | This platform's onboarding milestone. |
| `is_test_user` | boolean | Gates `#TestCourse` visibility. Always `false` on a fresh account - set by an admin. |

**`profile_status` IS NOT the token's `miles.onboarding_required`.** That claim describes the identity store -
whether the SSO still needs a name before it considers the account known - and it is a boolean of the
**opposite polarity**. A user can be fully known to the SSO and still be `new_user` here. Reading one for the
other is how a sign-up gate ends up inverted.

Failure modes, and each wants different UI:

| HTTP | Body | Meaning | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 401 | SSO's | Wrong or expired code. | Let them retype. |
| 429 | SSO's | Too many failures; the identifier is locked. | Show the lockout, do not retry. |
| 403 | `code: "account_blocked"` | Partner-imposed block. | **Terminal.** Show a permission message, not a login screen. Point at Miles support. |
| 403 | `code: "account_deactivated"` | Miles deactivation. | **Terminal.** Same, different team. |

**Replaces legacy MilesOne** `POST refresh`

POST - exchange a refresh token for a new session.

Body template generated from `AuthTokenRefreshRequestSerializerV1`. Values are placeholders, not fixtures.

Some values are ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES rather than placeholders - set `login_identifier` once and the three sign-in requests all read it. `refresh_token` is written by a script; do not type it.

**This request carries its own test script** on top of the collection-level one - open the Scripts tab to read what it writes into the environment.

---

> From `ACCOUNTS_API_CONTRACT_V1.md` - the contract the frontend web team works to.



### 2.4 `POST auth-token-refresh/` - rotate the session

Serves both client shapes:

```json
{ "refreshToken": "..." }   // app clients
{}                          // web clients - the httpOnly cookie is forwarded upstream
```

`refreshToken` is optional for exactly that reason; requiring it would lock every browser out of refresh.

The same two local flags (`profile_status`, `is_test_user`) are merged into a 200 here, and **they matter more
on this route than on verify.**

**THE ONBOARDING SEQUENCE, which is the single most common integration bug on this surface:**

1. A first-time user verifies and comes back `profile_status: "new_user"`.
2. They complete the profile (section 4).
3. **You must refresh the token.** The claim is minted with the token, so skipping the refresh re-reads a stale
   value and bounces the user straight back into onboarding they just finished.

Two more rules:

- **Refresh before expiry, not after a 401.** The access token is deliberately short - it is the window in
  which a suspended user keeps access, and it cannot be revoked once issued.
- **Never run two refreshes concurrently.** Refresh tokens rotate and the old one dies about ten seconds after
  use, so parallel refreshes invalidate the caller's own session. Serialise them behind one in-flight request.

A `401` from this route (`"Session could not be refreshed. Please sign in again."`) means the refreshed token
would not resolve to a local row - the account is gone or deactivated. Send them to sign-in.

## 10. Lead capture - three routes that file a Salesforce enquiry

**THERE WERE SIX UNTIL 2026-09-29, AND FIVE UNTIL 2026-09-30.** Two collapses, for the same reason
each time. `POST api/v1/caira/enquire-now/` is RETIRED and answers 404: it filed the same kind of lead
as `account/enquiry/` and differed only in naming CAIRA, so the programme moved into that endpoint's
body - see 10.1. The three `*/brochure-download/` routes are likewise RETIRED and answer 404; they
differed only in which programme the URL named, so that moved to a query parameter - see 10.2.

A brochure download is still its own endpoint rather than a fourth `programme` value on
`account/enquiry/`, because it pushes a Netcore event and answers "a brochure was downloaded", not
"somebody enquired".

All three take a JWT, POST only, and answer the SAME envelope. **None of them proxies Salesforce's
response body**, which is a deliberate change from legacy: returning `response.json()` straight through
made the CRM's schema part of this contract and leaked internal lead ids to a handset.

```json
{ "message": "Your request has been received. Our team will be in touch.", "status": "Success" }
```

- `200` - Salesforce accepted the lead.
- `502` - Salesforce refused or was unreachable. `{"message": "This service is temporarily unavailable,
  please try again later.", "status": "Failed"}`.

The learner is always taken from the token, never from the body.

### 10.1 The two contact routes

| Route | Body |
| --- | --- |
| `POST account/talk-to-us/` | none - pinned to US CPA, as legacy did |
| `POST account/enquiry/` | `programme`, plus an optional `lead` block |

`talk-to-us` starts the learner's **pathway-driven** webinar auto-registration, which fans out to
every audience their `user.pathway` implies - up to three webinars.

#### `POST account/enquiry/` - one route, every programme

```json
{
  "programme": "CPA",
  "lead": {
    "comment": "Asked about CMA pricing from the pricing page",
    "is_referral": true,
    "referrer_uuid": "99999999-8888-7777-6666-555555555555"
  }
}
```

`lead` is optional and so is every field in it. **The ordinary call is `{"programme": "CAIRA"}`.**

| field | type | required | what `null` means |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `programme` | `CPA` \| `CMA` \| `USP` \| `CAIRA` | **yes** | - absent is a 400 |
| `lead.comment` | string, max 500 | no | keep the flow's own comment |
| `lead.is_referral` | bool | no | keep the flow's own value |
| `lead.referrer_uuid` | uuid | no | forwarded to Salesforce as `null` |

**`programme` replaced `course_id` on 2026-09-29 and the old field is now a 400.** `course_id` made
the client state Salesforce's own id, so this contract moved whenever the remote catalogue did. The id
is resolved server-side now.

**What each programme does downstream.** They are not uniform, and the differences are the two
endpoints this route merged:

| `programme` | Salesforce `course_id` | `is_referral` | Webinars booked |
| --- | ---: | --- | --- |
| `CPA` | 1 | `true` | pathway fan-out - **up to 3** |
| `CMA` | 2 | `true` | pathway fan-out - **up to 3** |
| `USP` | 3 | `true` | pathway fan-out - **up to 3** |
| `CAIRA` | **18** | `false` | exactly **1** - the CAIRA audience |

**CAIRA files under course 18 as of 2026-09-29, and that is a change.** The retired
`caira/enquire-now/` sent no course id at all, so a CAIRA enquiry filed against whatever the learner's
pathway implied - course 1 for anyone with an empty pathway. It had no choice: the route took no body,
so nothing carried the programme into the payload. The body states it now, and 18 is the CRM's own id
for CAIRA. **Any report that counted CAIRA enquiries by course id must look at 18 from this date.**

**Identity and `campaign_id` are NOT accepted in `lead`** - they are a 400, not ignored. The learner
comes from the token, or a caller could file a lead against somebody else; `campaign_id` decides which
Salesforce campaign the lead lands in.

### 10.3 What happens after the 200

The Salesforce lead is **awaited** - you are told whether it was recorded. The webinar booking and the
Netcore push are **detached**, and their outcome is not in the status code. A 200 means the lead was
filed; it does not mean a seat was confirmed.

Auto-registration fires even when Salesforce refused. A CRM outage is not a reason to withhold a
webinar seat from a learner who just expressed interest.

### 8.1 `faqs/` is public on purpose, and now says so

Its docstring used to claim "JWT required" while the code served anyone - it declared an authenticator but no
permission class, and **declaring an `authentication_classes` does not require authentication**: without a
permission class DRF falls back to `AllowAny`. The same defect was found and fixed on `questions/` on
2026-09-09.

Resolved on 2026-09-17 by making the intent explicit rather than by adding a token check: FAQs are help content
on a pre-login screen, and the maintainer's decision is that they stay open. The authenticator was removed
entirely, so a **stale or expired token can no longer 403 the FAQ list** - which is what would have happened
had the declaration simply been left in place beside an `AllowAny`.

an explicit check in the handler, so they do refuse anonymous callers - with a 401 rather than a 403.

### 4.1 READ THIS FIRST: `profile/` changed meaning on 2026-09-09

Until 2026-09-09, `api/v1/account/profile/` served the **user row**. It does not any more - that is
`user_details/` (section 3). `profile/` now reads **questionnaire answers and nothing else**.

The rename was done deliberately while there was only one claimant, so the two never shared a name. If you have
code written against the old `profile/`, it is now pointing at a different resource that will return a
completely different shape.

### 4.3 `GET profile/` - the caller's answers

```json
{ "highest_qualification": "CA", "years_experience": 3, "interests": ["AI", "Audit"] }
```

A **bare map keyed by question code**, and the value is the answer itself - not an object describing it. Text
gives a string, select formats give a list, booleans give `true`/`false`, numbers give a number. An empty
answer set is `{}`, not a 404: having answered nothing is a normal state.

Flattened on 2026-09-10 from `{"type", "value", "choice_value"}` per code. **`type` is no longer reported
here** - join `questions/` on `code` if you need it.

Key order is the display order. There is no separate ordering field in the response.

### 4.1 READ THIS FIRST: `profile/` changed meaning on 2026-09-09

### 4.4 `PATCH profile/` - write them back

Query: `?form=onboarding` (default) or `?form=profile` - it names which milestone is in scope.

Body: the **same flat map** the GET returns, so you read, edit and send back without reshaping.

```json
{ "highest_qualification": "CA", "years_experience": 3 }
```

- **Partial by definition.** A code you omit is left exactly as it was, so a user can fill half a form, leave,
  and come back. This is why it is PATCH and not PUT.
- **`null` is refused**, not read as "clear". There is no clearing requirement yet and inventing one would fix
  that meaning forever.
- **Idempotent.** The same body twice yields the same rows and the same milestone. A retry after a mobile
  timeout is safe.

Response:

```json
{
  "answers": { },
  "profile_status": "onboard_completed",
  "is_onboarding_completed": true,
  "is_profile_completed": false,
  "missing": []
}
```

`answers` is the same flat map, nested rather than top-level because a bare map keyed by question code has
nowhere safe to carry metadata - a `profile_status` key would collide with a question coded `profile_status`.

**The write always succeeds; the milestone advances only when every required, shown question of that form has
an answer.** A partial save comes back with `missing` naming what is still outstanding rather than failing. Do
not treat a non-empty `missing` as an error.

A 400 is keyed by question code, one message per bad answer. Validation runs before the transaction opens, so a
rejected submission never partially applies.

**After this advances the milestone, refresh the token** - see 2.4.

The maintenance override: read it, set it, clear it. STAFF WRITE.

---

> From `ACCOUNTS_API_CONTRACT_V1.md` - the contract the frontend web team works to.



### 6.3 `account/universal/maintainance-status/` - the override

**GET is public** and reports the override plus what each surface is consequently serving:

```json
{
  "override_active": true,
  "override_value": true,
  "app": { "is_maintenance": true, "source": "cache" },
  "web": { "is_maintenance": true, "source": "cache" }
}
```

`source` is `cache` when a live override decided it and `env` when the surface fell back to its own
secret. It reports per surface because with no override live there is no single answer: the two
surfaces read two different secrets and can legitimately differ.

**POST requires a STAFF token.** It sets a cache override that outranks BOTH secrets for up to 7 days,
so it is gated on `is_staff` rather than on merely being signed in - there are far more learners than
there are people who should be able to take the platform down. A signed-in non-staff caller gets 403.

```json
{ "value": true, "ttl_seconds": 3600 }
```

- `value` is **required and nullable**, and those are different things. `null` CLEARS the override so
  each surface falls back to its own secret; omitting the key is a 400.
- `ttl_seconds` is optional. Default 86400 (24h), clamped to [60, 604800].
- Any undeclared key is a 400 naming the field.

The response is the GET body plus `ttl_seconds` on a set, or `"cleared": true` on a clear.

**ONE OVERRIDE COVERS BOTH SURFACES** - that is what "universal" names. A single POST puts app and web
into maintenance together; there is no per-surface override and a flip cannot be aimed at one client.

Every set and clear is audit-logged with the acting staff account's id at WARNING severity. This is an
operations tool - do not build a learner-facing UI onto it.

response.name: 403 Forbidden (2) - A valid token that is not `is_staff`

## 3. `api/v1/account/user-details/` - post-logout routing

REWRITTEN 2026-09-24. This section used to document `UserDetailsViewV1` and its 28-field user row on
`api/v1/account/user_details/` (underscore), **with a PATCH writing 16 of them**. That endpoint and that
view were DELETED. The hyphen spelling is now the only one, it is served by
`PathwayLogoutRouteViewV1`, and **there is no PATCH on it** - a client still sending one gets 405.

To write profile fields, use `PATCH account/profile/` (4.4).

### 3.1 `GET user-details/` - JWT

Answers, in one call, every independent question the app needs to pick a destination after login or
logout, so it does not make five round trips to decide one thing.

```json
{
  "first_name": "Sohan",
  "full_name": "Sohan Biswas",
  "is_onboarding_completed": true,
  "is_profile_completed": true,
  "Pathway": "Yes",
  "Enrolled_status": "Yes",
  "Enrolled_course": ["US CPA"],
  "onboarding_fully_completed": true
}
```

| Key | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `first_name` | Display name. Falls back to the first token of `full_name`. |
| `full_name` | Stored full name, whitespace-stripped. |
| `is_onboarding_completed` | The stored column. |
| `is_profile_completed` | The stored column. |
| `Pathway` | `"Yes"` / `"No"` - **a string, not a boolean**, and capitalised. Legacy's shape. |
| `Enrolled_status` | `"Yes"` / `"No"`, same caveat. |
| `Enrolled_course` | List of programme names. Empty list when not enrolled. |
| `onboarding_fully_completed` | DERIVED - every always-asked onboarding field is filled. Not the same as `is_onboarding_completed`, which is a stored flag. See 8.4. |

**`show_referral_code` MOVED TO `GET account/profile/` on 2026-09-24.** It is a property of the learner,
not of where to route them, and no routing decision read it. CLIENT VISIBLE.

**`career_counselling_booked`, `office_visit_booked` and `show_seven_day_challenge` were REMOVED** on the
same day. If you read any of the four, move or drop the read before deploying.

**A read failure degrades rather than fails.** If the enrolment lookup cannot be completed the endpoint
answers 200 with the conservative payload - `"Pathway": "No"`, `"Enrolled_status": "No"`,
`"Enrolled_course": []` - because a routing endpoint that 500s leaves the app with nowhere to send the
learner. Treat "No" as "we could not confirm", not as proof of absence.

### 8.4 `profile_status` has three values, and two booleans say the same thing

`profile_status`, `is_onboarding_completed` and `is_profile_completed` all encode the same two milestones and
all three are returned. They are consistent; the booleans exist because they are cheaper to branch on. None is
writable.

Mobile maintenance probe. ``GET app-api/v1/account/maintainance-status/``.

---

> From `ACCOUNTS_API_CONTRACT_V1.md` - the contract the frontend web team works to.



### 6.1 `GET app/maintainance-status/` - public

```json
{ "is_maintenance": false, "force_logout_all_user": false }
```

Is the **mobile** surface down. No `Authorization` header is inspected at all, so a stale token can
never stop a client reading the maintenance flag - which is exactly the client most likely to be
asking. Deliberately trivial, so it is safe to poll on every cold start.

`force_logout_all_user` **mirrors `is_maintenance` exactly** today: maintenance on means clear the
session and go to login, off means do not. It is a separate key because the two answer different
questions - "show the maintenance screen" and "discard this session" - and they are only equal for
now. Read both; do not infer one from the other, or the day a maintenance window is declared that
does not invalidate sessions, your build will be wrong and this endpoint will not.

### 6.4 Where the values come from, and why a secret edit is not enough

Both fall-back values load through AWS Secrets Manager (`APP_UNDER_MAINTENANCE`,
`WEB_APP_UNDER_MAINTENANCE`) and are read **once at process boot**. Editing a secret therefore changes
nothing until the service restarts. The override on 6.3 is the only live switch.

```
GET app|web/maintainance-status/
  -> Redis override live?  yes -> that value           source: cache
                            no -> this surface's secret source: env
```

---

\r\n \r\n \r\n

Episode 1: AI in the Audit Workflow 

Agentive. A company focused on building AI tools designed specifically for audit workflows. Its goal is to reduce repetitive manual work and improve efficiency through purpose-built software.

Assertions. Statements or claims that management makes in financial records and reports, which auditors evaluate during testing. Common examples include accuracy, cutoff, and classification.

Audit workflow. The sequence of steps, tasks, and procedures followed during an audit engagement. It includes activities like requesting documents, testing transactions, reviewing support, and documenting conclusions.

Burnout. A state of physical or mental exhaustion caused by prolonged stress, overload, or repetitive work demands. In professional settings, it often reduces motivation, focus, and long-term job satisfaction.

Citation-based. A method of review or analysis that ties findings back to specific source material or supporting evidence. This approach improves traceability and helps make conclusions easier to verify.

Classification. The process of assigning financial transactions to the correct categories in accounting records and reports. Proper classification helps ensure information is organized accurately and presented clearly.

Cutoff. An accounting concept used to determine whether transactions are recorded in the correct reporting period. It helps ensure income and expenses are recognized at the right time.

Expense testing. An audit procedure used to examine recorded expenses and verify that they are valid, accurate, and properly supported. It helps identify errors, misstatements, or compliance issues in expense-related transactions.

Financial statement review. A structured examination of financial statements to identify inconsistencies, risks, or potential issues. It often involves checking disclosures, presentation, and alignment with supporting records.

Grant revenue testing. An audit procedure used to verify that grant-related income is recorded correctly and supported by appropriate documentation. It helps confirm that revenue recognition follows the relevant terms and requirements.

Product design. The process of planning and developing products that solve user problems effectively and efficiently. It combines functionality, usability, and user needs to shape how a tool works in practice.

Repeatable. Describes a consistently performed process across different tasks or engagements. Repeatable methods improve reliability, efficiency, and standardization.

Episode 2 : AI Agents, Not Chatbots, for Audit

Agentic workflows. Structured AI-driven processes that carry out a sequence of connected tasks rather than answering a single prompt. They are designed to follow steps, use evidence, and move through a workflow in a more operational way.

Billable time. The hours a professional records and charges to a client for work performed. It is often used to measure effort, cost, and engagement profitability.

Client friction. Difficulty, delay, or frustration experienced by clients during a process or interaction. It often appears when requests are unclear, repetitive, or harder to complete.

Client portal. A secure digital space where clients can upload files, view requests, and exchange information with a service provider. It helps centralize communication and document sharing.

Core audit platform. The primary software system used by a firm to manage audit work, documentation, and engagement processes. It acts as the main operational base for carrying out audit procedures.

Evidence gathering. The process of collecting documents, records, and supporting information needed to evaluate whether a procedure or conclusion is supported. It is a key part of validating results and identifying exceptions.

Exceptions. Items or results that do not match expectations, criteria, or supporting records during a review or test. They are flagged for further examination because they may indicate an error, inconsistency, or risk.

General ledger. The central record that contains a company\u2019s financial transactions organized by account. It serves as a foundation for preparing reports and verifying financial activity.

Materiality. A threshold used to judge whether an item, error, or omission is significant enough to influence understanding or decisions. It helps determine what deserves closer attention in financial review.

Multi-step tool use. The ability of software or AI to complete a task through several connected actions rather than a single response. This can include extracting data, comparing values, checking conditions, and returning results.

Professional judgment. The informed decision-making that relies on expertise, experience, and careful evaluation of facts and circumstances. It is essential when interpreting results, assessing risks, and reaching conclusions.

Request list. A structured list of documents or information that a client is asked to provide for a review or engagement. A clear request list improves efficiency by making expectations easier to understand and fulfill.

Episode 3: Grant Revenue Testing in Agentive

Bulk upload. A feature that allows multiple files or documents to be uploaded at the same time instead of one by one. It helps speed up document collection and makes large-scale processing more efficient.

Conditional evidence. Supporting documentation used to determine whether specific requirements or conditions have been met. It helps verify timing, fulfillment, and related criteria tied to a transaction or agreement.

Contributions. Resources such as cash or other assets given to an organization without an equal exchange in return. They are often provided to support a purpose, program, or initiative.

Deep analysis. A more intensive review process that examines information in greater detail to generate richer findings or conclusions.
Donor-imposed restrictions. Limitations placed by a donor on how funds or assets may be used by the recipient. These restrictions help define the purpose, timing, or conditions attached to a contribution.

Grant agreement. A formal document that outlines the terms, amount, purpose, and conditions of a grant. It serves as a key source for understanding what was awarded and how it should be supported.

OCR. Short for optical character recognition, a technology that converts text in scanned files or images into readable digital text. It makes document contents searchable and easier for software to analyze.

Prompt injection. A technique used to insert referenced values or instructions into a prompt so the system can evaluate a specific item dynamically. It allows the same logic to adapt based on changing inputs or records.

Sampling. A method of selecting a portion of items from a larger group for review or testing. It is used to examine representative items without evaluating every single entry.

Selections. Chosen transactions, records, or items pulled from a larger data set for testing or review. They act as the specific entries against which supporting documents and procedures are applied.

Tick mark legend. A reference guide that explains the meaning of symbols or marks used in a work paper or review file. It helps users interpret whether items passed, failed, or require further attention.

Work paper. A document or file used to record procedures performed, evidence reviewed, and conclusions reached during a professional engagement. 

Episode 4 : Expense Testing in Agentive

Bank statements. Financial records provided by a bank that show deposits, withdrawals, and other account activity over a period of time. They help confirm whether recorded transactions were actually processed through the account.

Calendar year. A twelve-month period that runs from January 1 through December 31. It is often used as a standard time frame for organizing records, reporting activity, and checking whether entries fall in the correct period.

Counter evidence. Information that suggests a result may not match as expected or that raises doubt about a conclusion. It is useful in review because it highlights areas that may require closer attention or follow-up.

Fiscal year. A twelve-month accounting period used for tracking financial activity and reporting results. It may match the calendar year or follow a different start and end date depending on the organization.

Invoice. A document issued by a seller that lists goods or services provided and the amount owed. It serves as supporting evidence for charges, dates, vendors, and payment details.

Journal entry. A formal record used to enter financial transactions into an accounting system. It typically includes accounts affected, amounts, dates, and descriptions that help track how a transaction was recorded.

Match results. The output showing whether related records or documents have been linked successfully based on selected criteria. These results help users see if supporting files appear to correspond to the transaction being reviewed.

Operating expense. A cost incurred through the normal day-to-day running of an organization or business. Examples can include travel, software, meals, training, or hosting expenses tied to routine operations.

Reasoning. The explanation behind how a result, conclusion, or recommendation was reached. In a review process, reasoning helps users understand the logic used and its soundness.

Receipt check number. A numeric reference associated with a payment or transaction record that helps identify and connect it to supporting documentation. It can be used to trace activity across receipts, statements, and internal records.

Software expenses. Costs related to software products or services used by an organization, such as subscriptions, platforms, or digital tools.
Vendor name. The name of the supplier or business that provided a product or service. It is an important identifying detail used to match documents and confirm who a transaction relates to.

Episode 5: Financial Statement Review in Agentive

Batch email updates. Automated email summaries sent at set intervals to keep team members informed about comments, changes, or review activity. They help people stay aligned without needing to check the system constantly.

Column header. A label at the top of a column that identifies the type of data shown beneath it. It helps organize information and makes comparisons across values easier and more consistent.

Comparative statements. Financial statements that present figures from more than one period side by side for comparison. They help readers identify changes, trends, and inconsistencies across reporting periods.

Cross-footing. A process of checking whether totals remain accurate when values are added across rows and columns in a financial table. It helps confirm that different parts of a statement mathematically agree with one another.

Internal consistency. The degree to which the same information matches throughout a single document. It helps ensure that repeated figures, labels, and references do not conflict with each other.

Mathematical accuracy. The correctness of calculations, totals, and numeric relationships within a document or data set. It is essential for ensuring that reported values are reliable and free from arithmetic error.

Members equity. The residual interest in an organization\u2019s assets after liabilities are considered, often shown in statements for certain entity types. It reflects the accumulated value attributable to the members of the organization.

Prior year consistency. A check to confirm that values carried forward or presented comparatively from an earlier year still match the previously reported figures. It supports continuity and reduces the chance of mismatched historical numbers.

Review checklist. A structured list of items used to guide and document a review process. It helps ensure important checks are completed in a consistent and organized way.

Rounding error. A small difference in a number caused by rounding values up or down during calculation or presentation. While often minor, it can still create visible inconsistencies in reports and statements.

Row heading. A label placed beside a row to identify the category or line item associated with the values in that row. It provides context for interpreting the numbers across a table or statement.


Episode 6: Why AI-Native Audit Tools Win

Architectural reality. The practical limitations and constraints created by the way a software system is originally designed. It reflects how deeply the structure of a platform affects what can be added, changed, or improved later.

Backwards compatibility. The ability of newer software or systems to continue working with older data, features, or processes. It is often important for large platforms that need to avoid disrupting existing users and workflows.

Busy season. A period of especially high workload when teams face tighter deadlines, heavier volumes, and greater pressure. It often tests the efficiency of systems, staffing, and day-to-day processes.

Client experience. The overall impression and quality of interaction a client has while working with a company, service, or team. It is shaped by responsiveness, clarity, efficiency, and ease of collaboration.

Coverage. The extent to which a process, review, or system examines the full range of relevant items, risks, or activities. Greater coverage can improve confidence that important areas have been addressed.

Data models. Structured ways of organizing information so software can store, connect, and use it effectively. They shape how data moves through a system and how easily new capabilities can be built on top of it.

Distribution. The process or mechanism through which a product, platform, or service reaches its users or customers. In business strategy, strong distribution can be a major advantage because it affects adoption and market reach.

Incumbents. Established companies or providers that already hold a strong position in a market or industry. They often have scale, existing customers, and mature products, but may move more slowly than newer entrants.

Ingested. Processed and brought into a system so the information can be read, organized, and used. In digital workflows, documents or data are ingested before they can be analyzed or connected to other tasks.

Retention crisis. A situation in which an organization or industry struggles to keep people over time. It usually signals deeper problems related to workload, tools, satisfaction, or long-term career sustainability.

Startup. A newly built company created to solve a specific problem, often with a focus on speed, experimentation, and innovation. Startups typically operate with concentrated resources and a narrower mission than large established firms.

Switching costs. The time, effort, expense, or disruption involved in moving from one product, platform, or provider to another. High switching costs can make organizations hesitate even when better options become available.

**Module:** `EventsPage.views`  
**Route name:** `events-register-via-zoom-status-v1`

**Permission:** IsAuthenticated

**Replaces legacy MilesOne** `GET registerV4/<attempt_id>/status/`

``GET events/register-via-zoom-status-v1/<uuid:attempt_id>/``.

---

> From `EVENTS_API_CONTRACT_V1.md` - the contract the frontend web team works to.



## 3. `GET api/v1/events/register-via-zoom-status/<uuid:attempt_id>/`

The polling half of the handshake. Authenticated. Shared web + app. Takes NO query parameters - any query
string at all is a 400.

Scoped to the calling user, so one user cannot read another's attempt. A foreign or unknown id is
`404 attempt_not_found` rather than 403, which avoids confirming the id exists.

### 3.1 `200 OK`

```json
{
  "attempt_id": "9c2f1b70-8e4d-4a11-93cc-0d5a6f2e8b31",
  "status": "SUCCESS",
  "registration_status": "REGISTERED",
  "zoom_attempts": 1,
  "last_status_code": 201,
  "error_message": null,
  "error_code": null,
  "mf_retry_count": 0,
  "join_url": "https://us06web.zoom.us/w/8412...",
  "registered_email": "learner@example.com",
  "booking_id": "b41e77a2-1cf9-4c02-9c6e-3a8d5e0f1b22",
  "completed_at": "2026-09-17T09:14:22.118Z"
}
```

| Field | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `attempt_id` | UUID string | Echo of the path parameter. |
| `status` | string | The TEN-state internal status. Diagnostic, for Ops and support. Do not branch on it. |
| `registration_status` | string | The THREE-state client contract. Branch on this. |
| `zoom_attempts` | integer | How many times the Zoom leg has been tried. |
| `last_status_code` | integer or null | Last HTTP status seen from the external leg. |
| `error_message` | string or null | Human-readable reason. Safe to surface. |
| `error_code` | string or null | Machine-readable reason. |
| `mf_retry_count` | integer | Salesforce/MF forward retries. |
| `join_url` | string or null | The learner's own Zoom join URL. Populated once Zoom has issued it. |
| `registered_email` | string or null | The address this attempt actually sent to Zoom. On a FAILED attempt this is the only record of it, because the pipeline reads the profile live and the learner may have edited it since. This is the attendance-matching key. |
| `booking_id` | UUID string or null | Set once the `Booking` row exists. |
| `completed_at` | ISO-8601 string or null | Set when the attempt reached a terminal state. |

### 3.2 The three-state contract

`registration_status` is always one of:

| Value | Meaning | What the UI should do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PENDING` | Still working, or waiting on the Zoom host to approve the registrant. | Keep the spinner. Keep polling. |
| `REGISTERED` | The user IS registered on Zoom and holds a join URL. | Show the join affordance. Stop polling. |
| `REGISTER` | The pipeline stopped before a usable registration existed. | Show the retry CTA. Stop polling. |

The internal `status` collapses onto it like this:

| Internal `status` | `registration_status` |
| --- | --- |
| `SUCCESS` | `REGISTERED` |
| `MF_FAILED` | `REGISTERED` |
| `MF_PERMANENTLY_FAILED` | `REGISTERED` |
| `MF_SKIPPED` | `REGISTERED` |
| `ZOOM_FAILED` | `REGISTER` |
| `BOOKING_FAILED` | `REGISTER` |
| `INTERRUPTED` | `REGISTER` |
| `PENDING` | `PENDING` |
| `ZOOM_RETRYING` | `PENDING` |
| `ZOOM_PENDING_APPROVAL` | `PENDING` |

Two of these are worth understanding rather than just mapping:

- THE FOUR `MF_*` STATES ARE `REGISTERED`, not failures the user can act on. The Salesforce forward is an audit
  hand-off downstream of the fact that Zoom accepted the registrant. Telling the user to register again would
  be wrong AND would spend another Zoom registrant slot.
- `ZOOM_PENDING_APPROVAL` IS TERMINAL BUT MAPS TO `PENDING`. The Zoom host has to approve the registrant before
  a join URL is issued, and there is no action the user can take. A retry CTA there would invite a duplicate
  registration that Zoom answers with the same 409. The reason for the wait travels in `error_message` - show
  it. Note that polling this one will never resolve on its own timescale; see 4.2.

An unrecognised internal status collapses to `PENDING`, which is the safe default: a spinner rather than an
invitation to register twice.

### 3.3 Self-healing poll

If the worker handling an attempt died mid-pipeline (deploy, restart, crash), the row would otherwise sit
non-terminal forever and this endpoint would answer `PENDING` indefinitely - a spinner with nothing behind it.
Polling is exactly where that becomes observable, so it is where it is resolved: a stale attempt is reaped on
read and comes back as `INTERRUPTED` -> `REGISTER`, with

```
error_code: "stuck"
error_message: "The registration worker stopped before finishing (deploy, restart or crash).
                No Zoom registration was completed - please try again."
```

No cron has to have run for the client to get an actionable answer. Treat `REGISTER` as a genuine retry
affordance in this case - no Zoom registration was completed.

### 3.4 Refusals

| HTTP | `code` | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 400 | `invalid_request` | Any query parameter at all was sent. |
| 404 | `attempt_not_found` | No such attempt for this user. |

---

## 4. Driving the pair

### 4.1 The loop

1. `POST register-via-zoom/`.
2. `200` -> already registered, done. `202` -> take `attempt_id` and `status_url`.
3. Poll `status_url` until `registration_status` leaves `PENDING`.
4. `REGISTERED` -> show join, using `join_url`. `REGISTER` -> show retry, using `error_message`.

A sensible cadence is roughly every 2 seconds for the first 15 seconds, then back off. The happy path usually
resolves in a second or two; the pathological path is around 8 seconds of backoff.

### 4.2 Bound the poll

`ZOOM_PENDING_APPROVAL` is terminal but reads as `PENDING`, so a loop with no ceiling will spin on it forever.
Cap the poll (30-45 seconds is comfortable), and on timeout fall back to reading `status` and `error_message`
from the last response rather than continuing. That is the one place the internal `status` is worth reading on
the client, and it is for display, not for branching.

### 4.3 Do not re-POST to check state

A re-POST is safe - it will answer `200 already_registered` or `202` with the existing attempt - but it takes
the lock and writes a log line for nothing. Poll the status route.

---

> From `EVENTS_API_CONTRACT_V1.md` - the contract the frontend web team works to.



## 2. `POST api/v1/events/register-via-zoom/`

Registers the authenticated caller for a webinar. Authenticated. Shared web + app.

This is a `202` handshake, not a synchronous registration. The endpoint answers immediately with an
`attempt_id`; the actual work - Zoom registrant, then `Booking` plus `BookingDetails`, then the Salesforce
forward - runs in the background. Poll the status route (section 3) for the outcome.

The reason is latency: the Zoom leg is three attempts with 1s and 3s backoff and the Salesforce leg is another
three, so a worst case that still ENDS IN SUCCESS is around six round trips and roughly 8 seconds. That is not
a request to hold open.

### 2.1 Request body

```json
{
  "webinar_id": "3f1a9c7e-5b42-4d9a-8f10-2c6be7d41a55"
}
```

| Field | Type | Required | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `webinar_id` | UUID | yes | The `Events.Webinar` PRIMARY KEY. Not the MF/SF integer id. |

ONE FIELD, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE BODY. Nothing else is accepted - see 1.3.

THE WEBINAR IS ADDRESSED BY UUID, which is a change from legacy. Legacy took the producing service's integer
and resolved it as `(webinar_id, webinar_type)` - a compound lookup, because that integer is unique only in
combination with the type. An integer-only lookup here would either need the type threaded through the client
contract or would silently resolve to whichever row Postgres returned first. Whatever feed hands you a webinar
should expose its `id`; `webinar-main-page` (section 6) does.

ONE INPUT SURFACE. Legacy read each parameter from the query string first and fell back to the JSON body. Here
the body is canonical - a query parameter on this route is a 400.

### 2.2 `202 Accepted` - the normal answer

```json
{
  "status": "accepted",
  "registration_status": "PENDING",
  "message": "Registration started. Pull to refresh.",
  "attempt_id": "9c2f1b70-8e4d-4a11-93cc-0d5a6f2e8b31",
  "status_url": "/api/v1/events/register-via-zoom-status/9c2f1b70-8e4d-4a11-93cc-0d5a6f2e8b31/"
}
```

`status_url` is built server-side off the URLconf, so it cannot drift from the real route. Prefer following it
over assembling the path yourself.

### 2.3 `200 OK` - already registered

Not an error. The caller already holds a live booking for this webinar, and NO pipeline is spawned.

```json
{
  "status": "already_registered",
  "code": "already_registered",
  "message": "You are already registered for this webinar.",
  "booking_id": "b41e77a2-1cf9-4c02-9c6e-3a8d5e0f1b22"
}
```

### 2.4 Idempotency, in two layers

The expensive mistake here is a duplicate Zoom registrant, so a double-tap is absorbed rather than refused:

1. A LIVE BOOKING -> `200 already_registered` (section 2.3).
2. AN IN-FLIGHT ATTEMPT (`PENDING` or `ZOOM_RETRYING`) -> `202` carrying THAT attempt's id, with
   `message: "Registration already in progress."` Poll the one already running; do not start a second.

A third guard sits under both: a short per-`(user, webinar)` lock. If two taps land inside the same few
milliseconds, the loser gets `409 registration_in_progress` with `retry_after_seconds`. Retry once after that
and you will get the in-flight `202`.

### 2.5 Every refusal

| HTTP | `code` | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 400 | `invalid_request` | Body failed validation, or carried an undeclared key. Carries `errors[]`. |
| 400 | `missing_email` | The user's profile has no email. Zoom requires one. |
| 400 | `invalid_email` | Profile email is malformed. |
| 400 | `missing_first_name` | Profile has no first name. |
| 400 | `invalid_first_name` | First name contains non-ASCII - in practice an emoji pasted into a profile. Zoom rejects it with a terminal 400. |
| 404 | `webinar_not_found` | No such webinar row. |
| 409 | `unsupported_webinar_type` | The row is not a `webinar` or an `offline` event. Orientations and premiers have their own flows. |
| 409 | `webinar_inactive` | Soft-deleted or temporarily deactivated. 409 AND NOT 404 DELIBERATELY - the row exists and your copy of it is not wrong, so do not discard the webinar; it may come back. |
| 409 | `webinar_cancelled` | The session was cancelled. A cancelled webinar stays `active=True`, so this is a separate flag rather than a variant of the one above. |
| 409 | `webinar_start_time_missing` | The webinar has no scheduled start time yet. An ops data problem, not a client error - surface `detail` and let the user retry later. |
| 409 | `registration_in_progress` | Lock contention. Carries `retry_after_seconds` (currently 15). Retry once. |

The four profile refusals are worth handling specifically: each `detail` is already written as user-facing copy
naming what to fix in the profile, and none is retryable without that fix. They are checked BEFORE any Zoom
call, so the user learns synchronously instead of polling to a terminal failure.

Order of evaluation, which is the order you will hit them: body validation -> webinar resolution (404 / the
four 409s) -> profile preflight (the four 400s) -> idempotency (200 / 202) -> lock contention (409).

### 2.6 `offline` webinars take the identical path

An in-person event still goes through the full Zoom -> Booking -> Salesforce write path, and the learner still
gets a Zoom registrant record and a join URL - they simply do not use it. No client branch is needed.

## 5. `GET app-api/v1/events/all-bookings/`

Every booking the calling user holds. Authenticated. App only; the web twin is not built.

**MOVED FROM `web-api/v1/events/all-bookings/` ON 2026-09-17.** Same view, same response, same route name
(`events-all-bookings-v1`) - only the prefix changed. There is no redirect.

`Booking` is one table serving two things under a database-level XOR: a row either points at a webinar or
carries a 1:1 `booking_type`, never both and never neither. This endpoint returns BOTH sides, each row tagged
with its `kind`.

### 5.1 Query parameters

| Param | Type | Default | Values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `window` | string | `all` | `all`, `upcoming`, `past` |

There is deliberately NO `kind` filter: both kinds come from one table in one query, so filtering server-side
would save no work, and you already receive them pre-bucketed.

Any other parameter is a 400.

### 5.2 Response

```json
{
  "message": "Bookings retrieved successfully.",
  "data": {
    "upcoming": { "webinar": [], "one_on_one": [] },
    "past": { "webinar": [], "one_on_one": [] }
  }
}
```

`data.upcoming` is present only when `window` is `all` or `upcoming`; `data.past` only when `window` is `all`
or `past`. Both inner keys are always present when their window is, empty rather than omitted.

THE SPLIT POINT IS NOW MINUS 30 MINUTES, not now. A session that is running right now still reads as
`upcoming` while the user is in it.

A booking with no start time is filed under `upcoming` and sorts to the top. That is not a bug: a booking we
cannot date is not yet KNOWN to be past, and it needs attention.

Cancelled bookings never appear on either side.

### 5.3 One row

```json
{
  "kind": "webinar",
  "booking": {
    "id": "b41e77a2-1cf9-4c02-9c6e-3a8d5e0f1b22",
    "booking_type": null,
    "booking_type_label": null,
    "active_till": "2026-09-20T13:30:00Z",
    "status": true,
    "mf_log": true,
    "created_at": "2026-09-17T09:14:20.004Z",
    "attended_status": "1",
    "poll_questions_answered": 3,
    "total_poll_questions_available": 4,
    "total_webinar_duration_seconds": 3600,
    "attended_webinar_duration_seconds": 3240,
    "force_override_by_leadership_team": false
  },
  "details": {
    "id": "0f2b...",
    "book_id": "MF-99812",
    "datetime": "2026-09-20T13:00:00Z",
    "booking_url": "https://us06web.zoom.us/w/8412...",
    "registered_email": "learner@example.com",
    "spoc_name": null,
    "spoc_phone": null,
    "gmeet_link": null,
    "calendar_id": null
  },
  "webinar": { }
}
```

`booking` object:

| Key | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | UUID string | |
| `booking_type` | string or null | `null` on a webinar booking. One of `career` / `office` / `resume` / `alumni` on a 1:1. |
| `booking_type_label` | string or null | The human label for the same value - `Career Counselling`, `Office Visit`, `Resume Review`, `Alumni Connect`. Carried so you never map a code to a label yourself; re-deriving it client-side is how two surfaces end up wording one workflow differently. |
| `active_till` | ISO-8601 or null | The booking's effective time. For a webinar this is its start time. This is the ONLY column the upcoming/past split reads. |
| `status` | boolean | Always `true` in this feed - cancelled bookings are filtered out. |
| `mf_log` | boolean or null | The registration was forwarded to MF / Salesforce. Pipeline bookkeeping. |
| `created_at` | ISO-8601 | |
| `attended_status` | string | One-character MF code. See 5.4. |
| `poll_questions_answered` | integer | Written by the poll ingest, so `0` on a fresh booking. |
| `total_poll_questions_available` | integer | |
| `total_webinar_duration_seconds` | integer | **SECONDS.** Named `total_webinar_duration`
  until 2026-09-27; it was always seconds, so the RENAME carries no value change. |
| `attended_webinar_duration_seconds` | integer | **SECONDS.** Named
  `attended_webinar_duration` until 2026-09-27; same rename, same values. This is the FACT that
  `WebinarDetails.required_attendance_seconds` is compared against. |
| `force_override_by_leadership_team` | boolean or null | Eligibility override. `null` when no details row exists, which reads as "no override". |

`details` object:

| Key | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | UUID string or null | Nullable in practice: a booking written before the pipeline became atomic can lack its companion row. |
| `book_id` | string or null | Booking id from the external source. |
| `datetime` | ISO-8601 or null | |
| `booking_url` | string or null | THE PER-USER ZOOM JOIN URL for a webinar booking - this is the field you want. `null` on a 1:1. See 8.3 on the key name. |
| `registered_email` | string or null | The address Zoom holds the registrant under. Surfaced because it is the attendance-matching key: when it disagrees with the user's current email, that IS the explanation for a missing attendance record. |
| `spoc_name` | string or null | 1:1 only. |
| `spoc_phone` | string or null | 1:1 only. |
| `gmeet_link` | string or null | 1:1 only. |
| `calendar_id` | string or null | 1:1 only. Google Calendar event id; a cancellation keys on it. |

`webinar` object - PRESENT ONLY WHEN `kind == "webinar"`. The key is omitted rather than null on a 1:1, so an
absent webinar cannot be mistaken for a broken one.

| Key | Type |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | UUID string |
| `webinar_id_as_per_mf_sf` | integer or null |
| `webinar_name` | string |
| `webinar_type` | string |
| `webinar_description` | string |
| `webinar_start_date_time` | ISO-8601 or null |
| `webinar_end_date_time` | ISO-8601 or null |
| `webinar_duration_seconds` | integer or null, SECONDS |
| `zoom_id` | string or null |
| `caira_check` | boolean |
| `non_caira_check` | boolean |
| `active` | boolean |
| `cancellation_status` | boolean |
| `horizontal_thumbnail` | URL string, `""` when unset |
| `vertical_thumbnail` | URL string, `""` when unset |
| `square_image` | URL string, `""` when unset |

Image keys resolve to full public URLs, or to an empty string. They are never null and never a bare storage
key.

### 5.4 `attended_status` codes

| Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `"1"` | Attended |
| `"2"` | Not attended |
| `"3"` | Registered (MF never advanced the row past registration) |
| `"4"` | Cancelled |
| `""` | MF has not reported on this booking yet |

Only `"1"` grants CPE / badge eligibility.

---

### 9.5 No badge / feedback overlay on `all-bookings` yet

The legacy `v2/allbookings` feed decorated every webinar card with a CPE / badge / feedback overlay. The CPE
half has moved - a webinar's credit is now the sum of its active fields of study, which `webinar-main-page`
already returns as `total_cpe_credits`. The BADGE and FEEDBACK overlay is outstanding work on `all-bookings`. It is
unbuilt, not blocked.

> From `EVENTS_API_CONTRACT_V1.md` - the contract the frontend web team works to.



## 7. `GET web-api/v1/events/webinar-details-page/`

One webinar, in full - the page behind a card on `webinar-main-page`. **The surface follows your request**:
authenticated gets post-login, anonymous gets pre-login. There is no `login_type` parameter.

### 7.1 Query parameters

| Param | Type | Required | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `webinar_id` | uuid | yes | the `id` a main-page card carries |

There is deliberately no `login_type`, and sending one is a 400 (`extra_forbidden`) like any undeclared
parameter. `webinar-main-page` takes it because a signed-in visitor may legitimately want to preview the
signed-out page, so there the surface is a real choice. Here your token already answers it, and a parameter
that could contradict the token would be a second source of truth for one fact.

The id is the UUID, never `webinar_id_as_per_mf_sf` - that integer is unique only when paired with
`webinar_type`, and nothing in this backend hands it to a client.

### 7.2 Response

```json
{
  "message": "Webinar details retrieved successfully.",
  "data": { "login_type": "post_login", "webinar": { } }
}
```

The webinar object carries `subject_details` and `level_details.level_id` exactly as the card does - they are
produced by the same function, so the two screens cannot disagree.

`login_type` is echoed and is `pre_login` or `post_login`. It is more useful here than on the feed: there you
chose it, here it was DERIVED, so the echo is how you confirm which surface you got - and therefore whether
`registration` is present - without inspecting your own token.

### 7.3 The webinar object

**It is exactly the card object from section 8, plus four keys.** Render this page from the card type you
already have; the extras are additive. The shared keys are produced by the same function that shapes the
feed, so they cannot drift.

| Key | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `description` | string \| null | The long-form page body; `short_description` is the one-liner. |
| `trailer_url` | string \| null | |
| `trailer_thumbnail_url` | string \| null | |
| `product` | object \| null | See below. Null as a whole when the webinar is tagged to no product. |

`product`:

| Key | Type |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | UUID string |
| `name` | string |
| `mini_description` | string \| null |
| `description` | string \| null |
| `horizontal_image` | string (url, `""` when unset) |
| `vertical_image` | string (url, `""` when unset) |
| `square_image` | string (url, `""` when unset) |

`registration` (section 8.1) is present **only on an authenticated request**, exactly as on the feed. An
anonymous caller has no registration to report, so the key is absent rather than null.

`eligible` (section 8.2) is deliberately NOT emitted. It is a property of a BOOKING, the feed attaches it
only on `completed_webinar`, and computing it here would be a second definition of eligibility.

### 7.4 `product` and `subject` are two different columns and may disagree

Both name a row of `Masterclass.Subject`, reached by two different paths, and this endpoint reports both
rather than picking a winner:

- **`subject`** (a string, on the card) is the subject reached THROUGH `caira_masterclass_level`. The feed has
  emitted it since 2026-09-09 and it is untouched, so the two screens agree.
- **`product`** (an object, detail page only) is `Webinar.subject`, the direct FK, whose help text calls it
  "the Miles product this webinar is sold under" and says it SUPERSEDES the `caira_check` /
  `non_caira_check` pair.

They are independent columns, so a webinar tagged to a level of one subject and sold under another reports
both, honestly, under two names. **Which one wins is an open maintainer decision** - see section 9.8. Until
it is taken, prefer `product` where you need the commercial programme and `subject` where you need to match
what the feed showed.

### 7.5 Refusals

| Status | When |
| --- | --- |
| `400` | `webinar_id` missing, not a uuid, or any undeclared parameter |
| `403` | a bad or expired token. A request with NO token is served the pre-login surface, not refused |
| `404` | no webinar with that id is visible on this surface |

**The 404 is deliberately ambiguous.** "No such id" and "an id you may not see" are the same answer, so the
endpoint cannot be used to discover which ids exist. Visibility is the feed's own filter - soft-deleted,
cancelled, wrong login state and test webinars are all excluded before the id is matched, so a row the feed
hides cannot be opened by guessing.

---

### 9.3 `details.booking_url` is the response key; the column is named something else

The column was renamed to `zoom_booking_url` on 2026-09-15 and moved to the `Booking` table. THE RESPONSE KEY
IS UNCHANGED AND WILL STAY `booking_url` in v1 - renaming it is a client-visible break and belongs in a
versioned change, not in a column rename. If you see `zoom_booking_url` in a schema document or a backend
discussion, it is the same value.

The same applies to `details.calendar_id`, whose column is now `google_calender_id`.

### 9.8 `product` and `subject` can disagree, and neither has been declared the winner

Described in full in section 7.4. `Webinar.subject` (emitted as `product`) and
`caira_masterclass_level.subject` (emitted as `subject`) are independent columns pointing at the same table.
The model's help text says the direct FK supersedes the `caira_check` / `non_caira_check` pair, which implies
it is the authoritative one - but the feed has emitted the level's subject since 2026-09-09 and changing that
is a breaking change for a shipped contract.

Both are therefore emitted, under two names, on the detail page only. Collapsing them into one key is a
maintainer decision that has not been taken.

---
